eight_stage_timeline: Stage 1: Oral Tradition Formation (9th-10th century estimated) — Oghuz communities create narrative corpus around Dede Korkut; preserves tribal values
Stage 2: Shamanic-to-Sufi Transformation (10th-14th centuries) — Religious conversion provides reframing mechanism; shamanic motifs retained but reinterpreted through Sufi lens
Stage 3: Early Written Attestation (14th century) — Rashid al-Din cites Dede Korkut; first documented written reference establishes literary legitimacy
Stage 4: Manuscript Fixation and Ottoman Redaction (14th-16th centuries) — Ottoman scribal culture ensures standardized copies; multiple manuscript traditions emerge
Stage 5: European Archival Preservation (17th-18th centuries) — Dresden manuscript enters European networks; geographic dispersal ensures preservation redundancy
Stage 6: Modern Scholarly Rediscovery (20th century, 1950s onward) — Vatican manuscript discovered; Turkish academic synthesis; Western scholarly interest validates research subject
Stage 7: UNESCO Institutional Validation (2018) — Multinational nomination; ICH inscription; international legitimation and legal protection framework
Stage 8: Contemporary Performance and Entertainment (1970s-2026 ongoing) — Film/TV adaptations + living minstrel tradition + digital performance platforms
d3_causal_linking.causal_synthesis: Oral transmission → Manuscript fixation → International circulation → Academic legitimation → Institutional validation → Contemporary performance. Each stage creates infrastructure enabling next; self-reinforcing institutional support loop.
d3_causal_linking.critical_causal_mechanism: INSTITUTIONAL_SUPPORT_LOOP — Without institutional support (archives, universities, UNESCO), oral tradition would dissipate within 2-3 generations; institutions enable century-to-millennial scale transmission

section_hooks.content: A thousand-year-old epic in four manuscripts across three continents. Dresden (16th century European archive), Vatican (discovered 1950), Gonbad (discovered 2018 in Iran, Turkmen variant), Bursa (Ottoman period). Same story, different hands, different centuries. This is how culture survives: redundancy across geography, transformation through transmission.

section_hooks.content: UNESCO recognized Dede Korkut as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2018—not as historical document but as LIVING TRADITION. Contemporary minstrels still perform with saz instruments. Film adaptations exist (1988 cartoon, 2007 live-action, 2012 TV series). This isn't museum artifact—it's working cultural practice, sustained by institutions AND communities.
